original_question: Every Finsler S^2 has at least one elliptic prime closed geodesic.
target_in_paper: Conjecture 2.2.3 (Long) in Section 2.2, "Finsler metrics on S^2": "Every Finsler S^2 has at least one elliptic prime closed geodesic."
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's exact target and in fact matches Conjecture 2.2.3 almost verbatim. It has the correct manifold (S^2), the correct quantifier (every), the correct existence claim (at least one), and the correct type of orbit sought (an elliptic prime closed geodesic). It also correctly does not add irreversibility, bumpiness, or finiteness assumptions, because Conjecture 2.2.3 itself has none.
missing_details: Replace the shorthand "Finsler S^2" by "a Finsler metric F on the 2-sphere S^2" to make the ambient object explicit.
Specify that the geodesic is a closed geodesic of the given Finsler metric F.
Specify that "prime" means not a nontrivial iterate of a shorter closed geodesic; this matters because the paper explicitly distinguishes closed geodesics from repetitions of the same one.
Spell out "elliptic" in the standard closed-geodesic sense, i.e. via the linearized Poincare return map of the closed geodesic.

Make explicit that no extra assumptions such as irreversibility, reversibility, bumpiness, or finiteness of the set of prime closed geodesics are part of the conjecture; such hypotheses appear only in neighboring conjectures or partial results.
refined_question: Does every Finsler metric F on the 2-sphere S^2 admit a prime closed geodesic c whose linearized Poincare return map is elliptic?
justification: The draft is best matched by Conjecture 2.2.3 in Section 2.2, not by the neighboring Conjecture 2.2.1 (the "exactly 2 or infinitely many" problem) or Conjecture 2.2.2 (hyperbolic implies infinitely many). Section 1 provides the paper's ambient notation for geodesics and closed geodesics, and the surrounding discussion in Section 2 makes clear that the conjecture concerns Finsler metrics on S^2 in full generality. The refinement stays faithful to the paper and only expands shorthand and standard terminology so the question is mathematically stand-alone.
